16	**Named for C2 (THAM KHẢO):** hook share +5.1 points, because the cold open carries the pile definition (S03.6–S03.7, C1 finding) so act 1 can open on a result; M2 47.3 s is within 5 % of 50 s (named, CHARTER §4); M8 = 1 sentence (at the limit). Checker rule note: era years (2002, 2009, 1990s) cannot be matched because they live only in claim ids — handled with WORD_EXEMPT (narration) and unquoted era labels (beats), as Episode 8 did.
17	
18	**Summary.** Cold open (stands alone, no "last time"): 0:00 paradox — over ten years, stocks outgrew home prices about 9 in 10 times (S01.1), so the viewer expects renting and investing to come out ahead (S01.2); Nina rents with $92,000 saved and one twin for each choice (S02.1); three facts that push against that expectation — with the renting twin holding cash, the buyer ended ahead about 3 in 4 times (S02.2, Nina-tied) · with the same money in stocks, only about half (S02.3) · over fifteen years cash kept the buyer ahead every time, stocks only about 1 in 5 (S03.1); Nina's question (S03.2, audience Q4); the promise as a paradox (S03.3); one spoken limit (S03.4); the street (S03.5); the renter's pile defined in one sentence + picture (S03.6–S03.7, C1 finding). Act 1: the first house, January 1991 — first spoken result 4 s after S03 (S04.2), then why (stocks almost quintupled, the pile = $92,000 + monthly gap), the competitor gap (fixed growth rates → the real record), the costs and the one assumption (rent tag), all after the first result. Act 2: walking the street with the pile in stocks — 1990s mostly lit, January 1991 the darkest, 16 starts around March 1999 where stocks lost, 2002 through 2007 none of 72, June 2006 darker; the pile sank below its start in 183 of 307 windows (peak: $54,310, she kept investing); the count 152 of 307 (core), 80 switched, none back; April 2012 still lit; 2009 through mid-2016 78 percent lit; fifteen years turns the street over. Act 3: the paradox resolved (the house grows on all $400,000, the pile starts at $92,000; the renter's catch-up = monthly gap + time) → no monthly gap: about 2 in 3; 1 percent fee: 55 percent; the rent tag decides (flip at about 5.1 percent, right on the 5 percent assumption; Census range on screen). Limits, scoreboard, the 0:00 street returns, hand-off to an open question, Nina's answer last.

Cold open S02.1, S02.2, S03.2; through the method S09.4 (her month is not on the street), S14 (the renting twin who kept investing), S22.1 (the tag on her door), S25 (answer). No counterweight characters (the two Episode 8 houses, June 2006 and April 2012, act as counterweights without new people). No `promise_character` (M6 = 0).

Recalled in words (claim on the line, no digits): S15.4 "that half is a count … not a promise" (meaning) · S17.2 "the half isn't spread evenly" (comparison across eras) · S19.1 the paradox question (stocks outgrow homes, yet half) · S22.2 / S22.5 "at 5 percent … almost exactly in half … the answer sits on the rent tag" (threshold: the half sits on the assumption) · S25.2 scoreboard · S25.5 Nina's "coin flip". 27

29

31	- Act 1: *What changes when the renter's pile is invested?* Turn S04.3 (the same first house flips from $48,410 ahead to $485,063 behind).
32	- Act 2: *How much of the street stays lit?* Turns S12.2 (none of 72), S14.3 (peak: the pile sinks, she keeps going), S15.2 (core: about half), S18.3 (fifteen years: about one in five).
33	- Act 3: *Why does the house still hold half, and what tips it?* Turns S19.2 (the base), S20.2 (no monthly gap), S22.3 (the tag); S25 answers S03.2.
34

36	
37	**Viewer questions answered (dossier): 4 of 5, main = Q4.**
38	- **Q4** (is the renter's money invested, and does it beat home equity?) → S03.6–S03.7 (the pile, invested), S04–S05 (first house), S09–S18 (the whole street, 10 and 15 years), S19–S21 (why; lump variant; fees), S25.
39	- **Q1** (cost once interest, taxes, insurance, maintenance count) → S07.3 (all counted), V7 card B07.
40	- **Q2** (different rates, prices, rents) → real rates/prices replayed S09–S17 (eras), S22 (the rent tag turned; Census range on screen).
41	- **Q3** (hidden costs) → S07.2–S07.3 (closing, selling 6 percent), S21.1–S21.2 (fees on the renter's side), S24.1 (taxes not counted).
42	- **Q5** (non-financial) → S23.2: named as not measured.
43	
44	**Competitor gap (one beat, no channel named):** S06.1–S06.3 — fixed growth rates give one answer and hide the order of good and bad years → every month replayed from the real record (B06).
45	
46	**Claim-risk applied (`numbers.md` "Luật nói"):** no advice: no imperatives, conclusions as "in X of Y start months, the buyer ended ahead" + counterweight (S04.4, S11.3, S15.4, S17.2, S21.3, S23.1); on screen B03 "Not advice to buy, rent or invest"; "history, not a forecast": S03.4 (only spoken limit in 0:00–1:00), S24.1; "US only": S24.1 + corner tag from B01; stocks "the whole US stock market", no index brand, "before fees and taxes" S08.2 + fee variant S21; no capital-gains or home taxes S24.1; discipline is an assumption: S03.7, S08.3, S14.4–S14.5; lump variant S20; rent tag is an assumption S08.1, S22.5; Census range on screen only (B33); stocks pile ≠ advice to buy stocks S23.1; illustrative people: badge + B03 "Nina and her twins: ILLUSTRATIVE · prices, rents, rates, stock returns: real"; episode not called "first"; Episode 8 referenced only as "last time" after the cold open (S07.1, S13.1, S16.1).
47	
48	**Advice-like word list:** none of should / need to / have to / better off / worth it / pays off / wins / beat / safe / risky / consider / make sure in narration or on screen. "invests"/"investing" only as description of the replay (S03.2 question, S08.3, S14.3, S20.1, S25.5).
49	
50	**Statements without a numbers.md number (qualitative, for REVIEWER):** S05.3 pile mechanics; S06.1–S06.2 competitor weakness; S11.3 the buyer kept paying down her loan; S12.4 buyers paid near the peak of home prices; twins kept buying through the market's fall; S16.3 April 2012 bought after prices had fallen; S17.3 low prices and rates at start; S18.4 longer stays give the pile time to compound; S19.3–S19.4 base effect; S21.3 any renter-side cost moves houses back toward the buyer (direction shown by the fee variant).

CAST/BANNED_NAMES unchanged.
53	
54	**Line format.** As Episode 8. Emotion tags (3): S03.2 `[worried]`, S14.3 `[serious]` (`{peak}`), S25.5 `[thoughtful]`. ASR: no hyphenated year ranges, no "%", no "minus"; "Census Bureau" in full.

S19.1 So how can stocks outgrow home prices almost every time, and the buyer still finish ahead in half? <!-- claims: share_stocks_beat_house_10y, share_buyer_ahead_stocks_10y -->

early = [r for r in rows if r['start'] < 60]
for r in early:
    if r['role'] not in ROLES:
        fail.append(f'{r["sid"]}: câu trong 0:00–1:00 thiếu vai')


def mconds(rs, name):
    out = {}
    h = next((r for r in rs if r['role'] == 'hook'), None)
    p = next((r for r in rs if r['role'] == 'promise'), None)
    q = next((r for r in rs if r['role'] == 'question'), None)
    out['M1'] = h['end'] if h else None
    out['M2'] = p['end'] if p else None
    out['M3'] = q['end'] if q else None
    blk, best, bstart = None, 0.0, None
    for r in rs:
        if r['start'] >= 60:
            break
        if r['role'] in ('constraint', 'define'):
            bstart = r['start'] if bstart is None else bstart
            best = max(best, min(r['next'], 60) - bstart)
        else:
            bstart = None
    out['M4'] = best
    # M5 (D-013): lần ĐẦU nhân vật (hoặc câu hook có người) xuất hiện kết thúc ≤ 45 s — không còn đòi sau lời hứa (lời hứa nay ≤ 50 s)
    ret = next((r for r in rs if r['role'] == 'hook' or any(c in r['text'] for c in CAST + ['buyers'])), None)
    out['M5'] = ret['end'] if ret else None
    # M6: mỗi lời hứa về nhân vật được trả (tên trong CAST xuất hiện) ≤ 90 s sau câu hứa; không có lời hứa → 0
    m6 = 0.0
    if CAST == [] and any(r['role'] == 'promise_character' for r in rs):
        m6 = None   # không đo được: điền CAST (hoặc --cast)
    for i, r in enumerate(rs):
        if r['role'] != 'promise_character' or m6 is None:
            continue
        pay = next((x for x in rs[i + 1:] if any(re.search(r'\b' + c + r'\b', x['text']) for c in CAST)), None)
        m6 = max(m6, (pay['start'] - r['end']) if pay else float('inf'))
    out['M6'] = m6
    # M7 (D-013, story §1.2): câu `fact` thứ 3 kết thúc ≤ 35 s; ít hơn 3 câu fact → không đạt
    facts = [r for r in rs if r['role'] == 'fact']
    out['M7'] = facts[2]['end'] if len(facts) >= 3 else None
    # M8 (D-013, story §1.5): ≤ 1 câu `constraint` (miễn trừ, ≤ 1 vế) trong 0:00–1:00; phần còn lại lên hình
    out['M8'] = float(sum(1 for r in rs if r['role'] == 'constraint' and r['start'] < 60))
    lim = {'M1': 5.0, 'M2': 50, 'M3': 40, 'M4': 10, 'M5': 45, 'M6': 90, 'M7': 35, 'M8': 1}
    res = []

+S05.1 In those ten years, a dollar in the whole US stock market grew almost five times. <!-- claims: stocks_growth_1991-01_10y, n_10y -->

+S06.1 A lot of rent-versus-buy math assumes one growth rate; this replays the real record, month by month. <!-- claims: — -->

+
+S07.1 Every cost of owning stays the same, and the card lists each one. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.5 -->

+
+=== ACT 2 — JOURNEY: walking the street with the pile in stocks ===
+
+>>> CHAPTER 3: "The lights go out" (on screen + YouTube chapter)
+
+## S08 — The tag on the door
+
+S08.1 The renting twin's rent is an assumption, the tag on her door: 5 percent of the price a year, as of July 2026, and later, that tag decides. <!-- claims: yield_anchor_pct, hpi_last -->
+S08.2 So, with the pile in stocks, how much of the street stays lit? <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->

+## S09 — The street
+
+S09.1 After ten years, a house is lit if the buying twin's equity, after selling costs, is bigger than the renting twin's pile. <!-- claims: n_10y -->
+S09.2 If the pile is bigger, the door goes dark. <!-- claims: — -->
+S09.3 That's 307 houses, from January 1991 to the last start with ten full years of data, July 2016. <!-- claims: n_10y, last_10y -->
+S09.4 Nina's own month isn't on the street; its ten years are still ahead of her. <!-- claims: n_10y; hold: 0.5 -->

+
+S10.1 Most of the 1990s houses stay lit: 67.6 percent of them. <!-- claims: era_1990s_share_stocks -->
+S10.2 But the darkest house on the whole street is the very first one, January 1991. <!-- claims: worst_start_stocks_10y -->
+S10.3 Its renting twin caught the long stock boom from its first month. <!-- claims: — -->
+
+## S11 — Where stocks went nowhere
+
+S11.1 A few years later, the market itself stalled. <!-- claims: — -->
+S11.2 In 16 start months around March 1999, a dollar in stocks was worth less than a dollar ten years on. <!-- claims: n_stocks_lost_10y, stocks_growth_worst_start_10y, n_10y -->
+S11.3 Those houses stay lit: the pile lost ground while the buyer kept paying down her loan. <!-- claims: — -->
+
+## S12 — 2002 through 2007
+
+S12.1 Then the street goes dark, and stays dark. <!-- claims: — -->
+S12.2 For starts from 2002 through 2007, the buyer ended ahead in none of 72. <!-- claims: era_2002-2007_share_stocks; hold: 1.0 -->
+S12.3 With cash, 6 of them had stayed lit; with stocks, those lights go out too. <!-- claims: era_2002-2007_share_cash -->
+S12.4 These buyers paid near the peak of home prices, while their twins kept buying stocks through the market's fall and rebound. <!-- claims: — -->
+
+## S13 — The darkest house from last time
+
+S13.1 June 2006 was the darkest house last time, with the pile in cash. <!-- claims: adv_2006-06_cash_10y -->
+S13.2 With stocks, that buyer ends ten years $261,689 behind. <!-- claims: adv_2006-06_stocks_10y, n_10y; hold: 1.5 -->
+S13.3 The dark house got darker. <!-- claims: —; hold: 0.5 -->
+
+>>> CHAPTER 4: "The pile that sank" (on screen + YouTube chapter)
+
+## S14 — Below where she started (discipline)
+
+S14.1 Dark doors don't mean the renting twins had an easy ride. <!-- claims: — -->

+S14.5 Real people sometimes stop, and a renter who sells in a crash is not on this street. <!-- claims: —; hold: 0.5 -->
+

+
+S15.1 So, after the whole walk, how many houses are lit? <!-- claims: — -->

+

+S16.2 With stocks, that buyer still ends $237,632 ahead. <!-- claims: adv_2012-04_stocks_10y -->

+
+S17.1 Starts from 2009 through mid-2016 are 78 percent lit. <!-- claims: era_2009-2016_share_stocks -->

+
+S18.1 Stay fifteen years instead of ten, and with stocks, most of the lights go out. <!-- claims: — -->

+
+S19.1 So how can stocks outgrow home prices about 9 in 10 times, and the buyer still finish ahead in half? <!-- claims: share_stocks_beat_house_10y, share_buyer_ahead_stocks_10y -->

+S19.3 The mortgage lets a slower thing grow on a much bigger base. <!-- claims: — -->
